messages.content: Write the engineering culture section of a careers page. Around 250 words.

output:
We ship on a small team, so mistakes surface fast — and so does credit. Code review happens in hours, not days. If a PR sits overnight, someone will ask why.

You'll touch production in your first week. We don't gate that behind tenure; we gate it behind tests and a second pair of eyes. Every engineer carries a pager rotation, including the people who wrote the original system — nobody gets to hand off the pain they caused.

We argue about architecture in writing, in the open, before we build. Design docs get real pushback, not rubber stamps. If you're wrong, someone will say so directly, and you're expected to do the same back. That only works because we separate the critique from the person — disagreement here doesn't linger.

Meetings are rare. Most days you'll go heads-down for long stretches with Slack muted, and that's fine — we measure output, not presence. When we do meet, it's because writing it down first wasn't enough.

We keep a blameless postmortem culture, but "blameless" doesn't mean vague. Every incident review names the specific gap — a missing alert, a skipped test, an assumption nobody checked — and someone owns closing it before the next sprint.

Refactoring is normal work, not a special request. If you see a mess on the way to your task, you're expected to leave it better, not file a ticket and move on.

If you'd rather ship something imperfect on Tuesday than something polished on Friday, you'll fit in here.
